Reference: Levinsohn and Petrin (2003)

Model Setting

The paper asks how to estimate production function parameters when input choices respond to a productivity shock that the firm observes and the econometrician does not. This simultaneity problem, raised by Marschak and Andrews (1944), makes ordinary least squares (OLS) biased: firms with a large positive shock use more inputs, so the regressors are correlated with the error. The investment proxy of Olley and Pakes (1996) controls for the shock by inverting the investment demand function, but it is only valid for plants with strictly positive investment. In plant-level data from developing countries this is restrictive, because adjustment costs make investment lumpy; in the Chilean data used here more than half of the plant-year observations report zero investment. The paper shows that an intermediate input (materials, electricity or fuels, the inputs usually subtracted out in a value-added production function) can serve as the proxy instead. Intermediate inputs are almost always positive, they are cheap to adjust and therefore respond to the whole productivity term, and, because they are not state variables, the condition that makes them a valid proxy follows from a static profit maximization problem and not from the firm's dynamic problem.

The estimator has two stages. The first stage is a partially linear regression of output on the freely variable inputs and a non-parametric function of the proxy and capital, which delivers the coefficients of the variable inputs other than the proxy. The second stage uses a first-order Markov process for productivity and timing assumptions to form moment conditions that identify the coefficients on capital and on the proxy itself. Applied to the four largest Chilean manufacturing industries for 1979 to 1986, the estimator gives lower coefficients on variable inputs and higher coefficients on capital than OLS, the pattern implied by simultaneity; the estimates do not depend on whether materials or electricity is the proxy; and tests reject the equality of the intermediate input estimates with fixed effects estimates in every industry.

Simultaneity and the Direction of OLS Biases

Firm iii produces at time ttt according to Yit=f(Xit,ϵit;β)Y_{it}=f(X_{it},\epsilon_{it};\beta)Yit​=f(Xit​,ϵit​;β), where XitX_{it}Xit​ contains inputs that are easily adjusted and inputs that evolve over time, and ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​ is a Hicks-neutral productivity shock. A simultaneity problem arises when XitX_{it}Xit​ and ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​ are contemporaneously correlated. With many inputs the biases of the OLS coefficients cannot in general be signed, but a production function in logs with one freely variable input litl_{it}lit​ (labour) and one quasi-fixed input kitk_{it}kit​ (capital) gives the intuition:

yit=β0+βllit+βkkit+ϵit(4.6.2.1)y_{it}=\beta_0+\beta_l l_{it}+\beta_k k_{it}+\epsilon_{it} \tag{4.6.2.1}yit​=β0​+βl​lit​+βk​kit​+ϵit​(4.6.2.1)

The OLS estimates of the two input coefficients are

β^l=βl+σ^k,kσ^l,ϵ−σ^l,kσ^k,ϵσ^l,lσ^k,k−σ^l,k2β^k=βk+σ^l,lσ^k,ϵ−σ^l,kσ^l,ϵσ^l,lσ^k,k−σ^l,k2(4.6.2.2)\begin{aligned} \hat{\beta}_l&=\beta_l+\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{k,\epsilon}}{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}^2} \\ \hat{\beta}_k&=\beta_k+\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,\epsilon}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}}{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}^2} \end{aligned} \tag{4.6.2.2}β^​l​β^​k​​=βl​+σ^l,l​σ^k,k​−σ^l,k2​σ^k,k​σ^l,ϵ​−σ^l,k​σ^k,ϵ​​=βk​+σ^l,l​σ^k,k​−σ^l,k2​σ^l,l​σ^k,ϵ​−σ^l,k​σ^l,ϵ​​​(4.6.2.2)

where σ^a,b\hat{\sigma}_{a,b}σ^a,b​ is the sample covariance between aaa and bbb. The denominator is positive, so the numerators sign the biases, and three cases follow. If only labour responds to the shock (σ^l,ϵ>0\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}>0σ^l,ϵ​>0) and capital is uncorrelated with labour, β^l\hat{\beta}_lβ^​l​ is biased up and β^k\hat{\beta}_kβ^​k​ is unbiased. If only labour responds to the shock and capital and labour are positively correlated, β^k\hat{\beta}_kβ^​k​ is in addition biased down. If both inputs are positively correlated with each other and labour is more strongly correlated with the shock than capital is, β^l\hat{\beta}_lβ^​l​ tends to overestimate βl\beta_lβl​ and β^k\hat{\beta}_kβ^​k​ usually underestimates βk\beta_kβk​. The last two cases are the relevant ones in short panels, where identification comes mainly from between-firm variation and capital and labour are highly correlated. The standard alternatives have their own costs. The within estimator (fixed effects) protects against time-invariant firm effects but discards the between-firm variation that identifies the coefficients of state variables. An instrumental variable (IV) estimator needs instruments correlated with inputs and uncorrelated with ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​; firm-level input prices are rarely observed, and lagged inputs are valid only if the lag is long enough to break the dependence on a serially correlated shock.

The Investment Proxy of Olley and Pakes

Dropping the firm index, write the production function in logs with a freely variable input ltl_tlt​ and the state variable capital ktk_tkt​:

yt=β0+βllt+βkkt+ωt+ηt(4.6.2.3)y_t=\beta_0+\beta_l l_t+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t+\eta_t \tag{4.6.2.3}yt​=β0​+βl​lt​+βk​kt​+ωt​+ηt​(4.6.2.3)

The error is split into a transmitted component ωt\omega_tωt​, a state variable that affects the firm's decision rules, and an i.i.d. component ηt\eta_tηt​ that has no effect on decisions. Investment is a function of the two state variables:

it=it(ωt,kt)(4.6.2.4)i_t=i_t(\omega_t,k_t) \tag{4.6.2.4}it​=it​(ωt​,kt​)(4.6.2.4)

When ωt\omega_tωt​ is stochastically increasing in its past values, Pakes (1996) proves that for firms choosing to invest, investment is strictly increasing in ωt\omega_tωt​. Monotonicity allows the inversion ωt=ωt(it,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(i_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(it​,kt​), so that

yt=βllt+ϕt(it,kt)+ηtϕt(it,kt)=β0+βkkt+ωt(it,kt)(4.6.2.5)\begin{aligned} y_t&=\beta_l l_t+\phi_t(i_t,k_t)+\eta_t \\ \phi_t(i_t,k_t)&=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t(i_t,k_t) \end{aligned} \tag{4.6.2.5}yt​ϕt​(it​,kt​)​=βl​lt​+ϕt​(it​,kt​)+ηt​=β0​+βk​kt​+ωt​(it​,kt​)​(4.6.2.5)

This is a partially linear model: linear in ltl_tlt​ and non-parametric in ϕt\phi_tϕt​. Olley and Pakes approximate ϕt\phi_tϕt​ with a fourth-order polynomial in iti_tit​ and ktk_tkt​. Following Robinson (1988), one can instead take the expectation of the first line conditional on (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​) and subtract it, using the fact that ηt\eta_tηt​ is mean independent of iti_tit​ and ktk_tkt​:

yt−E[yt∣it,kt]=βl(lt−E[lt∣it,kt])+ηt(4.6.2.6)y_t-E[y_t\mid i_t,k_t]=\beta_l\left(l_t-E[l_t\mid i_t,k_t]\right)+\eta_t \tag{4.6.2.6}yt​−E[yt​∣it​,kt​]=βl​(lt​−E[lt​∣it​,kt​])+ηt​(4.6.2.6)

No-intercept OLS on this equation is consistent for βl\beta_lβl​. Capital enters ϕt\phi_tϕt​ twice, so βk\beta_kβk​ requires more structure. Olley and Pakes assume that ωt\omega_tωt​ follows a first-order Markov process and that capital does not respond immediately to the innovation in productivity:

ξt=ωt−E[ωt∣ωt−1](4.6.2.7)\xi_t=\omega_t-E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}] \tag{4.6.2.7}ξt​=ωt​−E[ωt​∣ωt−1​](4.6.2.7)

With yt∗y_t^*yt∗​ denoting output net of labour's contribution,

yt∗=yt−βllt=β0+βkkt+E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ηt∗(4.6.2.8)y_t^*=y_t-\beta_l l_t=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\eta_t^* \tag{4.6.2.8}yt∗​=yt​−βl​lt​=β0​+βk​kt​+E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ηt∗​(4.6.2.8)

where ηt∗=ξt+ηt\eta_t^*=\xi_t+\eta_tηt∗​=ξt​+ηt​. Regressing yt∗y_t^*yt∗​ on ktk_tkt​ and a consistent estimate of E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​] gives a consistent estimate of βk\beta_kβk​, because both ξt\xi_tξt​ and ηt\eta_tηt​ are uncorrelated with ktk_tkt​; the constant β0\beta_0β0​ is not separately identified from the mean of E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​].

Investment is a control on a state variable and is costly to adjust, which creates two problems. First, the monotonicity condition fails at zero investment, so these observations are truncated; this is a loss of efficiency. Second, non-convex adjustment costs can produce kinks in the investment function, so that investment does not respond fully to the shock even when it is positive. If investment reaches a maximal level at a kink point ωˉt(kt)\bar{\omega}_t(k_t)ωˉt​(kt​), then for ωt≥ωˉt(kt)\omega_t\geq\bar{\omega}_t(k_t)ωt​≥ωˉt​(kt​) the error of the differenced first-stage equation becomes ηt+(ωt−ωˉt(kt))\eta_t+(\omega_t-\bar{\omega}_t(k_t))ηt​+(ωt​−ωˉt​(kt​)), which is correlated with ltl_tlt​. The same happens if investment is chosen knowing only a part ωˉt\bar{\omega}_tωˉt​ of ωt\omega_tωt​: the remainder ωt−ωˉt\omega_t-\bar{\omega}_tωt​−ωˉt​ stays in the error term.

Intermediate Inputs as Proxies

Add a second freely variable input ιt\iota_tιt​, the intermediate input, to the production function, which is now a gross-output (revenue) production function:

yt=β0+βllt+βkkt+βιιt+ωt+ηt(4.6.2.9)y_t=\beta_0+\beta_l l_t+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+\omega_t+\eta_t \tag{4.6.2.9}yt​=β0​+βl​lt​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+ωt​+ηt​(4.6.2.9)

The demand for the intermediate input depends on the two state variables:

ιt=ιt(ωt,kt)(4.6.2.10)\iota_t=\iota_t(\omega_t,k_t) \tag{4.6.2.10}ιt​=ιt​(ωt​,kt​)(4.6.2.10)

Two assumptions are built into this function. Input and output prices are common across firms, so they are suppressed, and there is no error in the input demand function. If the demand function is monotonic in ωt\omega_tωt​ for all relevant ktk_tkt​, it can be inverted to ωt=ωt(ιt,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(ιt​,kt​), and the intermediate input replaces investment in the non-parametric term:

ϕt(ιt,kt)=β0+βkkt+βιιt+ωt(ιt,kt)(4.6.2.11)\phi_t(\iota_t,k_t)=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t) \tag{4.6.2.11}ϕt​(ιt​,kt​)=β0​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+ωt​(ιt​,kt​)(4.6.2.11)

The first stage is unchanged and identifies βl\beta_lβl​. In the second stage the proxy now also enters the production function, so both βk\beta_kβk​ and βι\beta_\iotaβι​ remain to be identified:

yt∗=β0+βkkt+βιιt+E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ηt∗(4.6.2.12)y_t^*=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\eta_t^* \tag{4.6.2.12}yt∗​=β0​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ηt∗​(4.6.2.12)

For any candidate value of (βk,βι)(\beta_k,\beta_\iota)(βk​,βι​) one can compute ωt\omega_tωt​ from the first-stage estimate of ϕt\phi_tϕt​ and hence estimate E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]. Capital is still uncorrelated with ηt∗\eta_t^*ηt∗​, but the intermediate input is not, because it responds to ξt\xi_tξt​. The lagged intermediate input ιt−1\iota_{t-1}ιt−1​ is chosen before either component of ηt∗\eta_t^*ηt∗​ is realized, and it is correlated with ιt\iota_tιt​ through the persistence of ωt\omega_tωt​ and of firm size. Identification therefore rests on

E[ktηt∗]=0,E[ιt−1ηt∗]=0(4.6.2.13)E[k_t\eta_t^*]=0,\qquad E[\iota_{t-1}\eta_t^*]=0 \tag{4.6.2.13}E[kt​ηt∗​]=0,E[ιt−1​ηt∗​]=0(4.6.2.13)

The Monotonicity Condition

The proxy is valid if, conditional on capital, profit maximization leads more productive firms to use more of the intermediate input. Let the technology in levels be Y=f(K,L,ι,ω)Y=f(K,L,\iota,\omega)Y=f(K,L,ι,ω), twice continuously differentiable in labour LLL and the intermediate input ι\iotaι. The industry is competitive: firms take the input prices pLp_LpL​ and pιp_\iotapι​ and the output price, normalized to one, as given. Capital is fixed within the period (this period's investment either does not respond to this period's productivity or does not enter this period's capital), and productivity is observed before labour and the intermediate input are chosen. The firm maximizes f(K,L,ι,ω)−pLL−pιιf(K,L,\iota,\omega)-p_L L-p_\iota\iotaf(K,L,ι,ω)−pL​L−pι​ι, with first-order conditions

fL(K,L,ι,ω)=pL,fι(K,L,ι,ω)=pι(4.6.2.14)f_L(K,L,\iota,\omega)=p_L,\qquad f_\iota(K,L,\iota,\omega)=p_\iota \tag{4.6.2.14}fL​(K,L,ι,ω)=pL​,fι​(K,L,ι,ω)=pι​(4.6.2.14)

Differentiating both conditions with respect to ω\omegaω, holding capital and prices fixed, gives a linear system in the two responses:

fLL∂L∂ω+fιL∂ι∂ω+fLω=0fιL∂L∂ω+fιι∂ι∂ω+fιω=0(4.6.2.15)\begin{aligned} f_{LL}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\omega}+f_{\iota L}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}+f_{L\omega}&=0 \\ f_{\iota L}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\omega}+f_{\iota\iota}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}+f_{\iota\omega}&=0 \end{aligned} \tag{4.6.2.15}fLL​∂ω∂L​+fιL​∂ω∂ι​+fLω​fιL​∂ω∂L​+fιι​∂ω∂ι​+fιω​​=0=0​(4.6.2.15)

Solving for the response of the intermediate input,

∂ι∂ω=fιLfLω−fLLfιωfLLfιι−fιL2(4.6.2.16)\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}=\frac{f_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}}{f_{LL}f_{\iota\iota}-f_{\iota L}^2} \tag{4.6.2.16}∂ω∂ι​=fLL​fιι​−fιL2​fιL​fLω​−fLL​fιω​​(4.6.2.16)

The denominator is positive by the second-order condition of the firm's problem, so

sign(∂ι∂ω)=sign(fιLfLω−fLLfιω)(4.6.2.17)\text{sign}\left(\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}\right)=\text{sign}\left(f_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}\right) \tag{4.6.2.17}sign(∂ω∂ι​)=sign(fιL​fLω​−fLL​fιω​)(4.6.2.17)

The monotonicity result is: if fιLfLω>fLLfιωf_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}>f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}fιL​fLω​>fLL​fιω​ everywhere, the intermediate input demand function ι(ω;pL,pι,K)\iota(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)ι(ω;pL​,pι​,K) is strictly increasing in ω\omegaω. The proof integrates the derivative: for ω2>ω1\omega_2>\omega_1ω2​>ω1​,

ι(ω2;pL,pι,K)−ι(ω1;pL,pι,K)=∫ω1ω2∂ι∂ω(ω;pL,pι,K) dω>0(4.6.2.18)\iota(\omega_2;p_L,p_\iota,K)-\iota(\omega_1;p_L,p_\iota,K)=\int_{\omega_1}^{\omega_2}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)\,d\omega>0 \tag{4.6.2.18}ι(ω2​;pL​,pι​,K)−ι(ω1​;pL​,pι​,K)=∫ω1​ω2​​∂ω∂ι​(ω;pL​,pι​,K)dω>0(4.6.2.18)

The condition has a simple reading. Optimizing behaviour implies a declining marginal product of labour at chosen bundles, fLL<0f_{LL}<0fLL​<0. If productivity weakly raises the marginal product of every input, then fLω≥0f_{L\omega}\geq 0fLω​≥0 and fιω≥0f_{\iota\omega}\geq 0fιω​≥0, so the second term −fLLfιω-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}−fLL​fιω​ is non-negative, and it is strictly positive when fιω>0f_{\iota\omega}>0fιω​>0. The first term has the sign of the cross-partial fιLf_{\iota L}fιL​: if the marginal product of the intermediate input weakly rises with labour (fιL≥0f_{\iota L}\geq 0fιL​≥0) the condition holds, and if fιL<0f_{\iota L}<0fιL​<0 it may still hold depending on the relative size of the two products. The condition is immediate for Cobb-Douglas and can be checked directly for a constant elasticity of substitution technology. This is the practical advantage over investment: Pakes (1996) has to work through the dynamic problem to show monotonicity of investment, and any change to that model requires a new proof. Moreover, the estimator does not impose monotonicity, so it can be checked in the data. If input prices are observed and differ across firms they can be added as arguments of the demand function; if they are unobserved but thought to vary over time, regions or firm types, separate functions can be estimated for each group.

Data and Choice of Proxy

The data are the Chilean manufacturing census collected by the Instituto Nacional de Estadistica: 6665 plants with at least 10 employees, observed annually from 1979 to 1986, in an unbalanced panel that is not censored for entry and exit. The paper studies the four largest 3-digit industries excluding petroleum and refining: Food Products (ISIC 311), Metals (381), Textiles (321) and Wood Products (331), with 6115, 1394, 1129 and 1032 observations in the estimation. Output is gross revenue; labour is man-years, separately for skilled (white-collar) and unskilled (blue-collar) workers; the intermediate inputs are materials, electricity and fuels. All values are deflated to real 1980 Chilean pesos. Capital is the sum of depreciated buildings, machinery and vehicles, with depreciation rates of 5, 10 and 20 percent, each type jjj evolving as

Kjt=(1−δj)Kj,t−1+ijt,Kt=∑jKjt(4.6.2.19)K_{jt}=(1-\delta_j)K_{j,t-1}+i_{jt},\qquad K_t=\sum_j K_{jt} \tag{4.6.2.19}Kjt​=(1−δj​)Kj,t−1​+ijt​,Kt​=j∑​Kjt​(4.6.2.19)

Investment in this period enters capital in this period, unlike in Olley and Pakes, where last period's investment enters this period's capital. For capital to remain uncorrelated with ξt\xi_tξt​, today's investment must then be decided knowing only ωt−1\omega_{t-1}ωt−1​. The period contains a boom (1979 to 1981), the recession that followed the debt crisis (1982 to 1983) and a recovery (1984 to 1986); real GDP falls from 1134.7 in 1981 to 968.0 in 1983. The function ωt(ιt,kt)\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)ωt​(ιt​,kt​) is therefore allowed to differ across these three periods. The number of plants falls in every industry, for example from 1537 to 1288 in Food Products and from 524 to 313 in Wood Products.

The first criterion for a proxy is the share of non-zero observations, since zeros must be truncated. Investment is non-zero for 42.7, 44.8, 41.2 and 35.9 percent of observations in industries 311, 381, 321 and 331, against 8 percent of zeros in the data of Olley and Pakes. Materials are non-zero for 99.8, 99.9, 99.9 and 99.7 percent, electricity for 88.3, 96.5, 97.0 and 93.8 percent, and fuels for 78.0, 63.1, 51.2 and 59.3 percent. Two further criteria come from the assumptions. The demand function has no error, which is doubtful for electricity if unreliable supply makes observed use differ from demand. The non-parametric first stage is sensitive to measurement error, which is a concern for storable inputs such as materials and fuels, since purchases need not equal use; electricity cannot be stored, and its price was regulated at a common unit price for plants consuming less than 2 MW, which covers over 90 percent of the sample. Materials are the main proxy and electricity the alternative.

Three specification tests are proposed. The first plots the estimated ωt\omega_tωt​ against the proxy and capital and checks that it increases in the proxy for given capital. The second compares the estimates obtained with different proxies, which should agree for the variable inputs other than the proxy if the model is correct. The third is a test of over-identifying restrictions: inputs chosen in one period should be uncorrelated with the next period's innovation ξt+1\xi_{t+1}ξt+1​.

First Stage

The production function is approximated by a Cobb-Douglas technology with six inputs:

yt=β0+βkkt+βslts+βultu+βeet+βfft+βmmt+ωt+ηt(4.6.2.20)y_t=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_s l_t^s+\beta_u l_t^u+\beta_e e_t+\beta_f f_t+\beta_m m_t+\omega_t+\eta_t \tag{4.6.2.20}yt​=β0​+βk​kt​+βs​lts​+βu​ltu​+βe​et​+βf​ft​+βm​mt​+ωt​+ηt​(4.6.2.20)

where yty_tyt​ is the log of gross output, ktk_tkt​ the log of capital, ltsl_t^slts​ and ltul_t^ultu​ the logs of skilled and unskilled labour, and mtm_tmt​, ftf_tft​ and ete_tet​ the logs of materials, fuels and electricity. With materials as the proxy,

yt=βslts+βultu+βeet+βfft+ϕt(mt,kt)+ηtϕt(mt,kt)=β0+βmmt+βkkt+ωt(mt,kt)(4.6.2.21)\begin{aligned} y_t&=\beta_s l_t^s+\beta_u l_t^u+\beta_e e_t+\beta_f f_t+\phi_t(m_t,k_t)+\eta_t \\ \phi_t(m_t,k_t)&=\beta_0+\beta_m m_t+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t(m_t,k_t) \end{aligned} \tag{4.6.2.21}yt​ϕt​(mt​,kt​)​=βs​lts​+βu​ltu​+βe​et​+βf​ft​+ϕt​(mt​,kt​)+ηt​=β0​+βm​mt​+βk​kt​+ωt​(mt​,kt​)​(4.6.2.21)

This could be estimated by OLS with a polynomial in mtm_tmt​ and ktk_tkt​; a third-order polynomial gives very similar results. The paper instead estimates the conditional means of output and of the four variable inputs given (kt,mt)(k_t,m_t)(kt​,mt​) by locally weighted quadratic least squares, and subtracts the conditional expectation of the first line from itself:

yt−E(yt∣kt,mt)=βs(lts−E(lts∣kt,mt))+βu(ltu−E(ltu∣kt,mt))+βe(et−E(et∣kt,mt))+βf(ft−E(ft∣kt,mt))+ηt(4.6.2.22)\begin{aligned} y_t-E(y_t\mid k_t,m_t)={}&\beta_s\left(l_t^s-E(l_t^s\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\beta_u\left(l_t^u-E(l_t^u\mid k_t,m_t)\right) \\ &+\beta_e\left(e_t-E(e_t\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\beta_f\left(f_t-E(f_t\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\eta_t \end{aligned} \tag{4.6.2.22}yt​−E(yt​∣kt​,mt​)=​βs​(lts​−E(lts​∣kt​,mt​))+βu​(ltu​−E(ltu​∣kt​,mt​))+βe​(et​−E(et​∣kt​,mt​))+βf​(ft​−E(ft​∣kt​,mt​))+ηt​​(4.6.2.22)

No-intercept OLS on this equation gives β^s\hat{\beta}_sβ^​s​, β^u\hat{\beta}_uβ^​u​, β^e\hat{\beta}_eβ^​e​ and β^f\hat{\beta}_fβ^​f​. If only the marginal products of these inputs were of interest, estimation could stop here. The capital coefficient, plant-level productivity and returns to scale require the second stage, because both materials and capital enter ϕt\phi_tϕt​ twice.

Second Stage

Two moment conditions identify βm\beta_mβm​ and βk\beta_kβk​. Capital does not respond to the innovation in productivity, and last period's materials choice is uncorrelated with this period's innovation:

with the intercept suppressed. This requires separability only in the proxy input, which is weaker than what a value-added production function assumes for all the intermediate inputs that are subtracted out.

Bootstrap Inference and Alternative Estimators

The routine has 11 estimating equations and many estimates are used more than once, so analytical standard errors along the lines of Pakes and Olley (1995) are laborious. The paper uses the bootstrap. Each firm's full set of observations is treated as one independent draw; firms are sampled with replacement and with equal probability until the number of firm-year observations equals or just exceeds that of the original data. The whole routine is repeated on each of 200 samples. Because more moments than parameters are used, the bootstrapped moments are recentred by the values of the sample moments at the minimum of the objective function on the original data. The difference between two estimators is computed sample by sample, so its distribution accounts for the covariance between them. Standard errors, the distribution of the over-identification statistic and the tests comparing estimators all come from these samples.

The alternatives are OLS, fixed effects, IV with inputs lagged one period as instruments, the investment proxy of Olley and Pakes, the intermediate input estimator restricted to plants with positive investment, and the estimator of Blundell and Bond (2000), which starts from

yit=β′xit+γt+(ηi+vit+mit)(4.6.2.29)y_{it}=\beta' x_{it}+\gamma_t+(\eta_i+v_{it}+m_{it}) \tag{4.6.2.29}yit​=β′xit​+γt​+(ηi​+vit​+mit​)(4.6.2.29)

where γt\gamma_tγt​ is a time effect, ηi\eta_iηi​ a firm fixed effect, vitv_{it}vit​ an AR(1) shock and mitm_{it}mit​ an MA(0) measurement error. It uses inputs lagged at least two periods as instruments for the first-differenced equations and lagged first differences as instruments for the equations in levels. In the Chilean data its estimates were very sensitive to the bootstrap sample and often fell on the boundary of the parameter space, so they are not reported.

Results for Chilean Manufacturing

With materials as the proxy, the estimates for Food Products (311) are 0.139 for unskilled labour, 0.051 for skilled labour, 0.085 for electricity, 0.023 for fuels, 0.500 for materials and 0.240 for capital, with bootstrapped standard errors of 0.010, 0.009, 0.007, 0.004, 0.078 and 0.053. The materials coefficient is the largest in every industry (0.420 in Metals, 0.500 in Textiles and 0.550 in Wood Products), and the capital coefficients are 0.290, 0.180 and 0.190 in these three industries. All coefficients are significant at standard levels except electricity in Textiles (0.005 with a standard error of 0.019). Returns to scale, the sum of the six coefficients, are 1.037, 1.172, 1.007 and 1.133 in industries 311, 381, 321 and 331, with standard errors of 0.059, 0.075, 0.113 and 0.157, so constant returns are generally not rejected.

The specification tests are mostly passed. The plots of estimated productivity against materials and capital are increasing in materials in all three periods for the three largest industries, with some violations in Textiles in 1984 to 1986 at low materials use and high capital; for Wood Products the surfaces in the last two periods are irregular. Replacing materials by electricity changes the coefficients on unskilled labour, skilled labour and fuels by at most 0.011 in absolute value and the capital coefficient by 0.03, −0.03-0.03−0.03, 0.07 and 0.13 in the four industries; none of these differences is significant at the 10 percent level. The P-values of the over-identification test with the materials proxy are 0.01, 0.51, 0.86 and 0.68, and with the electricity proxy 0.00, 0.32, 0.10 and 0.40, so the restrictions are rejected only in Food Products, the industry with about five times as many observations as the others.

The comparison with OLS matches the predicted biases. In Food Products the OLS estimate minus the intermediate input (LP) estimate is 0.004 for unskilled labour, 0.011 for skilled labour, 0.011 for electricity, 0.001 for fuels, 0.210 for materials and −0.190-0.190−0.190 for capital; the OLS estimate is the larger one in 70, 100, 100, 77.5, 97 and 2.5 percent of the 200 bootstrap samples. Across the four industries, 15 of the 20 coefficients on variable inputs are larger under OLS, and the capital coefficient is smaller under OLS in every industry (differences of −0.190-0.190−0.190, −0.225-0.225−0.225, −0.141-0.141−0.141 and −0.112-0.112−0.112), so 19 of the 24 differences agree with the simultaneity story. Because the two biases offset each other, the effect on returns to scale is ambiguous: the OLS minus LP difference is 0.049, −0.056-0.056−0.056, 0.049 and −0.030-0.030−0.030. The differences between the Olley and Pakes estimates and the LP estimates in Food Products look similar to those for OLS, except for unskilled labour, which is consistent with the intermediate input responding more fully to the productivity shock than investment does.

Wald tests of the hypothesis that two estimators give the same parameter vector summarize the comparisons. In Food Products LP differs from OLS, fixed effects, IV, Olley and Pakes and LP on plants with positive investment, each with a P-value below 0.01; the only pair that does not differ is Olley and Pakes against LP on plants with positive investment (0.56). In Metals, Textiles and Wood Products the P-values for LP against OLS are 0.20, 0.58 and 0.21, against IV 0.22, 0.09 and below 0.01, against Olley and Pakes 0.54, 0.20 and 0.89, and against LP on plants with positive investment 0.02, 0.27 and 0.93. The rejection in the two largest industries of the equality between LP on all plants and LP on plants with positive investment indicates that truncating the zero-investment observations is not innocuous. Fixed effects is rejected against every other estimator in every industry at the 1 percent level, which says that the persistent shock correlated with input choices varies within firms over time and is not a fixed effect. The rejections against IV suggest that last period's inputs respond to the same unobserved shock as this period's inputs.

This is the log-linear (Cobb-Douglas) production function that the note uses to show in which direction OLS is biased. In levels it reads

Yit=eβ0LitβlKitβkeϵitY_{it}=e^{\beta_0}L_{it}^{\beta_l}K_{it}^{\beta_k}e^{\epsilon_{it}}Yit​=eβ0​Litβl​​Kitβk​​eϵit​

so that yity_{it}yit​, litl_{it}lit​ and kitk_{it}kit​ are the logs of output, labour and capital of firm iii in year ttt. The coefficients βl\beta_lβl​ and βk\beta_kβk​ are output elasticities: one percent more labour raises output by βl\beta_lβl​ percent. The term ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​ is a Hicks-neutral productivity shock, meaning that it scales output for given inputs and leaves the marginal rate of substitution between inputs unchanged. Labour is freely variable and capital is quasi-fixed.

The equation is not a regression in the usual sense because ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​ is (at least partly) known to the firm when it chooses inputs. A simple illustration: a price-taking firm with output price one and wage pLp_LpL​ sets the marginal product of labour βlYit/Lit\beta_l Y_{it}/L_{it}βl​Yit​/Lit​ equal to pLp_LpL​, which gives

lit=11−βl(β0+ln⁡βl−ln⁡pL+βkkit+ϵit)l_{it}=\frac{1}{1-\beta_l}\left(\beta_0+\ln\beta_l-\ln p_L+\beta_k k_{it}+\epsilon_{it}\right)lit​=1−βl​1​(β0​+lnβl​−lnpL​+βk​kit​+ϵit​)

Log labour therefore rises by 1/(1−βl)1/(1-\beta_l)1/(1−βl​) for each unit of the shock, and the regressor is correlated with the error. This is the simultaneity problem. Equation (2) uses this specification to sign the OLS biases, and equation (3) refines it by splitting ϵit\epsilon_{it}ϵit​ into a part the firm reacts to and pure noise.

Start from equation (1) and let all variables be measured as deviations from sample means, so that the constant drops out. The OLS normal equations for the two slopes, written with sample covariances, are

β^l=σ^k,kσ^l,y−σ^l,kσ^k,yσ^l,lσ^k,k−σ^l,k2,β^k=σ^l,lσ^k,y−σ^l,kσ^l,yσ^l,lσ^k,k−σ^l,k2\hat{\beta}_l=\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,y}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{k,y}}{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}^2},\qquad \hat{\beta}_k=\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,y}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,y}}{\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,k}-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}^2}β^​l​=σ^l,l​σ^k,k​−σ^l,k2​σ^k,k​σ^l,y​−σ^l,k​σ^k,y​​,β^​k​=σ^l,l​σ^k,k​−σ^l,k2​σ^l,l​σ^k,y​−σ^l,k​σ^l,y​​

Insert these into the numerator of the labour coefficient. The terms in βk\beta_kβk​ cancel and the terms in βl\beta_lβl​ reproduce the denominator:

Dividing both numerators by the common denominator yields the two lines of the target equation. The denominator is positive by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality whenever labour and capital are not perfectly collinear, so the numerators sign the biases.

The three cases in the note follow by inspection. If σ^l,ϵ>0\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}>0σ^l,ϵ​>0 and σ^k,ϵ=σ^l,k=0\hat{\sigma}_{k,\epsilon}=\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}=0σ^k,ϵ​=σ^l,k​=0, the labour bias is σ^l,ϵ/σ^l,l>0\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}/\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}>0σ^l,ϵ​/σ^l,l​>0 and the capital bias is zero. If σ^l,ϵ>0\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}>0σ^l,ϵ​>0, σ^k,ϵ=0\hat{\sigma}_{k,\epsilon}=0σ^k,ϵ​=0 and σ^l,k>0\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}>0σ^l,k​>0, the capital numerator is −σ^l,kσ^l,ϵ<0-\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}<0−σ^l,k​σ^l,ϵ​<0: capital is blamed for the output that the extra labour did not produce. If all three covariances are positive, the capital bias is negative exactly when σ^l,kσ^l,ϵ>σ^l,lσ^k,ϵ\hat{\sigma}_{l,k}\hat{\sigma}_{l,\epsilon}>\hat{\sigma}_{l,l}\hat{\sigma}_{k,\epsilon}σ^l,k​σ^l,ϵ​>σ^l,l​σ^k,ϵ​, which holds when labour is much more responsive to the shock than capital and the two inputs are strongly correlated; this is why the note says "usually" for that case.

This is the Olley and Pakes production function. Relative to equation (1) the firm index is dropped and the single error is split into two parts with different economic roles, ϵt=ωt+ηt\epsilon_t=\omega_t+\eta_tϵt​=ωt​+ηt​.

The transmitted component ωt\omega_tωt​ is productivity that the firm knows when it takes decisions. It is a state variable of the firm's dynamic problem, it is serially correlated, and it is the source of the simultaneity problem because the choice of ltl_tlt​ (and of investment) depends on it. The component ηt\eta_tηt​ is an i.i.d. shock that is realized after decisions are taken, or simply measurement error in output; it has no effect on any choice, so it is uncorrelated with all inputs. Both are in log units, so a value ωt=0.1\omega_t=0.1ωt​=0.1 means roughly ten percent more output from the same inputs.

The split is what makes a proxy approach possible. If one can find an observable that reveals ωt\omega_tωt​, as in equation (4), the remaining error ηt\eta_tηt​ is harmless and the coefficients of freely variable inputs can be estimated consistently, as in equation (6). The coefficient βl\beta_lβl​ belongs to an input chosen within the period, whereas βk\beta_kβk​ belongs to a state variable fixed before ωt\omega_tωt​'s innovation is known; this timing difference is used in equations (7) and (8). The constant β0\beta_0β0​ cannot be separated from the mean of ωt\omega_tωt​. The linear-in-logs form is a first-order approximation; nothing in the method needs it beyond additivity of ωt\omega_tωt​ and ηt\eta_tηt​.

This is the investment policy function from the firm's dynamic problem in Olley and Pakes. The firm enters period ttt with capital ktk_tkt​ and productivity ωt\omega_tωt​, and chooses investment iti_tit​ to maximize the expected discounted value of profits. Because (ωt,kt)(\omega_t,k_t)(ωt​,kt​) are the only state variables, the optimal choice is a function of these two only. The subscript ttt on the function allows it to shift over time with anything that is common to all firms in a period, such as input prices, demand conditions or market structure.

Three things are assumed by writing the equation this way. First, productivity is a scalar: there is no second unobservable that moves investment. Second, there is no error in the function, so two firms with the same (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​) in the same period must have the same ωt\omega_tωt​. Third, firm-specific prices or adjustment costs are excluded.

Pakes (1996) shows that if the distribution of future ω\omegaω is stochastically increasing in current ωt\omega_tωt​, then investment is strictly increasing in ωt\omega_tωt​ whenever it is positive. A strictly increasing function can be inverted:

ωt=ωt(it,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(i_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(it​,kt​)

This inverse expresses the unobservable as an unknown function of two observables and is substituted into the production function in equation (5). The restriction to it>0i_t>0it​>0 is the weakness that the paper addresses: at it=0i_t=0it​=0 many values of ωt\omega_tωt​ map to the same investment and the inversion fails. Equation (10) is the analogue with an intermediate input.

Start from the production function in equation (3) and the inverse of the investment function in equation (4), ωt=ωt(it,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(i_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(it​,kt​), which exists for observations with positive investment. Substituting the inverse for ωt\omega_tωt​ gives

yt=β0+βllt+βkkt+ωt(it,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_0+\beta_l l_t+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t(i_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=β0​+βl​lt​+βk​kt​+ωt​(it​,kt​)+ηt​

The function ωt(⋅)\omega_t(\cdot)ωt​(⋅) is unknown, so the linear term βkkt\beta_k k_tβk​kt​ and the constant cannot be told apart from it: any change in βk\beta_kβk​ can be offset by a change in how ωt(⋅)\omega_t(\cdot)ωt​(⋅) depends on ktk_tkt​. Collect everything that depends on (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​) only into one unknown function,

ϕt(it,kt)=β0+βkkt+ωt(it,kt)\phi_t(i_t,k_t)=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t(i_t,k_t)ϕt​(it​,kt​)=β0​+βk​kt​+ωt​(it​,kt​)

which is the second line of the target. With this definition the production function becomes

yt=βllt+ϕt(it,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_l l_t+\phi_t(i_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=βl​lt​+ϕt​(it​,kt​)+ηt​

which is the first line. The regressor ltl_tlt​ enters linearly and (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​) enter through an unrestricted function, so this is a partially linear model. The error is now only ηt\eta_tηt​, which is unrelated to all choices, so the simultaneity problem for ltl_tlt​ has been removed. The price is that βk\beta_kβk​ is not identified at this stage because capital appears twice inside ϕt\phi_tϕt​: once through its own productive contribution and once as an argument of the inverse investment function.

Start from the first line of equation (5) and take the expectation conditional on (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​). Three facts are used: βl\beta_lβl​ is a constant; ϕt(it,kt)\phi_t(i_t,k_t)ϕt​(it​,kt​) is a function of the conditioning variables, so its conditional expectation is itself; and ηt\eta_tηt​ is mean independent of (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​), so E[ηt∣it,kt]=0E[\eta_t\mid i_t,k_t]=0E[ηt​∣it​,kt​]=0. Hence

E[yt∣it,kt]=βlE[lt∣it,kt]+ϕt(it,kt)E[y_t\mid i_t,k_t]=\beta_l E[l_t\mid i_t,k_t]+\phi_t(i_t,k_t)E[yt​∣it​,kt​]=βl​E[lt​∣it​,kt​]+ϕt​(it​,kt​)

Subtract this from the first line of equation (5). The unknown function cancels:

yt−E[yt∣it,kt]=βllt+ϕt(it,kt)+ηt−βlE[lt∣it,kt]−ϕt(it,kt)=βl(lt−E[lt∣it,kt])+ηt\begin{aligned} y_t-E[y_t\mid i_t,k_t]&=\beta_l l_t+\phi_t(i_t,k_t)+\eta_t-\beta_l E[l_t\mid i_t,k_t]-\phi_t(i_t,k_t) \\ &=\beta_l\left(l_t-E[l_t\mid i_t,k_t]\right)+\eta_t \end{aligned}yt​−E[yt​∣it​,kt​]​=βl​lt​+ϕt​(it​,kt​)+ηt​−βl​E[lt​∣it​,kt​]−ϕt​(it​,kt​)=βl​(lt​−E[lt​∣it​,kt​])+ηt​​

which is the target. In practice the two conditional expectations are replaced by non-parametric regression estimates of yty_tyt​ and of ltl_tlt​ on (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​), and βl\beta_lβl​ is the slope of a no-intercept OLS regression of one residual on the other (Robinson, 1988). Because ηt\eta_tηt​ is uncorrelated with ltl_tlt​ and with any function of (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​), this regression is consistent.

An assumption that the note leaves unstated: the regression needs variation in lt−E[lt∣it,kt]l_t-E[l_t\mid i_t,k_t]lt​−E[lt​∣it​,kt​]. If labour is chosen as an exact function of the same state variables (ωt,kt)(\omega_t,k_t)(ωt​,kt​) and nothing else, then ltl_tlt​ is itself a function of (it,kt)(i_t,k_t)(it​,kt​), the residualized regressor is identically zero and βl\beta_lβl​ is not identified. This collinearity point was raised later by Ackerberg, Caves and Frazer; the first stage works only if something else (for example firm-specific wage variation or optimization error unrelated to ηt\eta_tηt​) moves labour.

This equation defines the innovation in productivity and, through it, states the assumption about how productivity evolves. Productivity follows a first-order Markov process: the distribution of ωt\omega_tωt​ given the whole past depends on ωt−1\omega_{t-1}ωt−1​ only. The conditional expectation E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​] is the part of today's productivity that the firm could forecast yesterday; it is an unrestricted function g(ωt−1)g(\omega_{t-1})g(ωt−1​), not necessarily linear. The innovation ξt\xi_tξt​ is the surprise, the part that becomes known only in period ttt.

By construction ξt\xi_tξt​ is mean independent of ωt−1\omega_{t-1}ωt−1​ and, under the Markov assumption, of everything the firm knew or chose in period t−1t-1t−1:

E[ξt∣ωt−1,kt−1,lt−1,…]=0E[\xi_t\mid\omega_{t-1},k_{t-1},l_{t-1},\ldots]=0E[ξt​∣ωt−1​,kt−1​,lt−1​,…]=0

A linear special case is the AR(1) process ωt=ρωt−1+ξt\omega_t=\rho\omega_{t-1}+\xi_tωt​=ρωt−1​+ξt​, for which E[ωt∣ωt−1]=ρωt−1E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]=\rho\omega_{t-1}E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]=ρωt−1​.

The decomposition matters because inputs differ in what they respond to. A freely variable input chosen in period ttt responds to all of ωt\omega_tωt​, including ξt\xi_tξt​. Capital is assumed to be determined before ξt\xi_tξt​ is known, so it can be correlated with the forecastable part E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​] but not with ξt\xi_tξt​. Controlling for the forecastable part and leaving ξt\xi_tξt​ in the error is the idea of the second stage in equation (8), and the orthogonality of ξt\xi_tξt​ to lagged choices generates the moment conditions in equations (13), (23) and (26).

Start from equation (3) and move the labour term, whose coefficient is known from the first stage in equation (6), to the left-hand side. This defines yt∗y_t^*yt∗​:

yt∗=yt−βllt=β0+βkkt+ωt+ηty_t^*=y_t-\beta_l l_t=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t+\eta_tyt∗​=yt​−βl​lt​=β0​+βk​kt​+ωt​+ηt​

Rearranging the definition of the innovation in equation (7) gives ωt=E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ξt\omega_t=E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\xi_tωt​=E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ξt​. Substitute this for ωt\omega_tωt​:

yt∗=β0+βkkt+E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ξt+ηty_t^*=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\xi_t+\eta_tyt∗​=β0​+βk​kt​+E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ξt​+ηt​

Collect the two unforecastable terms into one composite error, ηt∗=ξt+ηt\eta_t^*=\xi_t+\eta_tηt∗​=ξt​+ηt​, to obtain the target:

yt∗=β0+βkkt+E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ηt∗y_t^*=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\eta_t^*yt∗​=β0​+βk​kt​+E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ηt∗​

The point of the rewriting is that capital is correlated with ωt\omega_tωt​ but not with ηt∗\eta_t^*ηt∗​: ξt\xi_tξt​ is unknown when capital is determined, and ηt\eta_tηt​ never affects decisions. So once the forecastable part of productivity is controlled for, ktk_tkt​ is an exogenous regressor. The control is feasible because for any candidate βk\beta_kβk​ lagged productivity can be recovered from the first-stage function of equation (5) as ωt−1=ϕt−1−β0−βkkt−1\omega_{t-1}=\phi_{t-1}-\beta_0-\beta_k k_{t-1}ωt−1​=ϕt−1​−β0​−βk​kt−1​, and E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​] is then an unknown function of this quantity. Since that function is unrestricted, it absorbs any constant, which is why β0\beta_0β0​ is not separately identified.

This is the production function of the paper's own model: equation (3) with one more freely variable input, the intermediate input ιt\iota_tιt​ (in logs), with output elasticity βι\beta_\iotaβι​. Examples are materials, electricity and fuels.

Adding ιt\iota_tιt​ changes what yty_tyt​ measures. A value-added production function subtracts intermediate inputs from output before estimation; here they stay on the right-hand side, so yty_tyt​ is the log of gross output (measured as deflated revenue) and all coefficients are gross-output elasticities. They are smaller than value-added elasticities; for example, with a materials elasticity of 0.5, a capital elasticity of 0.24 in gross output corresponds to roughly 0.24/(1−0.5)=0.480.24/(1-0.5)=0.480.24/(1−0.5)=0.48 in value added.

The error structure is as in equation (3): ωt\omega_tωt​ is the transmitted, serially correlated productivity known to the firm, and ηt\eta_tηt​ is noise that affects no decision. Both ltl_tlt​ and ιt\iota_tιt​ are chosen after ωt\omega_tωt​ is observed, so both are correlated with it, while ktk_tkt​ is a state variable.

The intermediate input plays two roles. It is a regressor, with coefficient βι\beta_\iotaβι​, and through its demand function in equation (10) it is the proxy that reveals ωt\omega_tωt​. Because of this double role its coefficient cannot be estimated in the first stage and is carried into the non-parametric function in equation (11); it is recovered in the second stage, equation (12), together with βk\beta_kβk​. Equation (20) is the six-input version taken to the data.

This is the demand function for the intermediate input and the counterpart of the investment function in equation (4). It says that the quantity of the intermediate input chosen in period ttt depends on two things only: productivity ωt\omega_tωt​ and the capital stock ktk_tkt​.

The economic content is different from the investment case. The intermediate input is not a state variable; it is used up within the period and does not affect future profits. Its demand therefore comes from a static problem: given ktk_tkt​ and ωt\omega_tωt​, choose the variable inputs to maximize current profit. The solution depends on (ωt,kt)(\omega_t,k_t)(ωt​,kt​) and on prices. A Cobb-Douglas example in logs, with ctc_tct​ collecting constants and prices, is

ιt=ct+βk1−βl−βιkt+11−βl−βιωt\iota_t=c_t+\frac{\beta_k}{1-\beta_l-\beta_\iota}k_t+\frac{1}{1-\beta_l-\beta_\iota}\omega_tιt​=ct​+1−βl​−βι​βk​​kt​+1−βl​−βι​1​ωt​

which is linear and strictly increasing in ωt\omega_tωt​ when βl+βι<1\beta_l+\beta_\iota<1βl​+βι​<1.

Two assumptions are built in. Input and output prices are the same for all firms in a period, which is why they do not appear as arguments and why the function carries a subscript ttt. And there is no error term: two firms with the same (ιt,kt)(\iota_t,k_t)(ιt​,kt​) have the same ωt\omega_tωt​. If the function is strictly monotonic in ωt\omega_tωt​ for every relevant ktk_tkt​, it can be inverted to ωt=ωt(ιt,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(ιt​,kt​), used in equation (11). The condition under which monotonicity holds is derived in equations (14) to (18). The advantages over investment are that intermediate inputs are almost never zero and face no adjustment costs.

Start from the production function in equation (9). Under monotonicity, the demand function in equation (10) can be inverted to ωt=ωt(ιt,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(ιt​,kt​). Substitute this for ωt\omega_tωt​:

yt=β0+βllt+βkkt+βιιt+ωt(ιt,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_0+\beta_l l_t+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=β0​+βl​lt​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+ωt​(ιt​,kt​)+ηt​

Now group the terms by what they depend on. The labour term depends on ltl_tlt​; the constant, the capital term, the intermediate input term and the inverted productivity all depend on (ιt,kt)(\iota_t,k_t)(ιt​,kt​) only. Define the sum of the latter as

ϕt(ιt,kt)=β0+βkkt+βιιt+ωt(ιt,kt)\phi_t(\iota_t,k_t)=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+\omega_t(\iota_t,k_t)ϕt​(ιt​,kt​)=β0​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+ωt​(ιt​,kt​)

which is the target. The production function is then yt=βllt+ϕt(ιt,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_l l_t+\phi_t(\iota_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=βl​lt​+ϕt​(ιt​,kt​)+ηt​, the same partially linear form as the first line of equation (5), and the first stage of equation (6) applies with (ιt,kt)(\iota_t,k_t)(ιt​,kt​) as conditioning variables.

The difference from equation (5) is the extra term βιιt\beta_\iota\iota_tβι​ιt​. In the investment case the proxy does not enter the production function; here it does, so both ιt\iota_tιt​ and ktk_tkt​ appear twice inside ϕt\phi_tϕt​, linearly and as arguments of the unknown function ωt(⋅)\omega_t(\cdot)ωt​(⋅). Neither βι\beta_\iotaβι​ nor βk\beta_kβk​ can be separated from that function in the first stage. What the first stage does deliver is an estimate of the whole function ϕt\phi_tϕt​, from which productivity can be backed out for any candidate coefficients as ωt=ϕt−β0−βkkt−βιιt\omega_t=\phi_t-\beta_0-\beta_k k_t-\beta_\iota\iota_tωt​=ϕt​−β0​−βk​kt​−βι​ιt​.

Start from equation (9) and subtract the labour term, whose coefficient the first stage has identified, so that yt∗=yt−βllty_t^*=y_t-\beta_l l_tyt∗​=yt​−βl​lt​:

yt∗=β0+βkkt+βιιt+ωt+ηty_t^*=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+\omega_t+\eta_tyt∗​=β0​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+ωt​+ηt​

Use the definition of the innovation in equation (7), ωt=E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ξt\omega_t=E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\xi_tωt​=E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ξt​:

yt∗=β0+βkkt+βιιt+E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ξt+ηty_t^*=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_\iota\iota_t+E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\xi_t+\eta_tyt∗​=β0​+βk​kt​+βι​ιt​+E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ξt​+ηt​

With ηt∗=ξt+ηt\eta_t^*=\xi_t+\eta_tηt∗​=ξt​+ηt​ this is the target equation. It is equation (8) plus the term βιιt\beta_\iota\iota_tβι​ιt​, which remains on the right-hand side because its coefficient was not identified in the first stage.

The conditional expectation is computable for any candidate (βk,βι)(\beta_k,\beta_\iota)(βk​,βι​). From equation (11), lagged productivity is ωt−1=ϕt−1−β0−βkkt−1−βιιt−1\omega_{t-1}=\phi_{t-1}-\beta_0-\beta_k k_{t-1}-\beta_\iota\iota_{t-1}ωt−1​=ϕt−1​−β0​−βk​kt−1​−βι​ιt−1​, and the forecast is an unknown function of it, estimated by a non-parametric regression.

The new difficulty is endogeneity of ιt\iota_tιt​. It is chosen after the firm sees all of ωt\omega_tωt​, so it responds to ξt\xi_tξt​ and is correlated with ηt∗\eta_t^*ηt∗​; least squares on this equation would overstate βι\beta_\iotaβι​. Capital remains uncorrelated with ηt∗\eta_t^*ηt∗​. One more exclusion restriction is needed for βι\beta_\iotaβι​, and equation (13) supplies it with the lagged intermediate input.

The two conditions follow from the timing of decisions and the definition ηt∗=ξt+ηt\eta_t^*=\xi_t+\eta_tηt∗​=ξt​+ηt​ used in equation (12).

Consider capital first. By assumption ktk_tkt​ is determined without knowledge of the innovation ξt\xi_tξt​, so it is a function of information dated t−1t-1t−1. Under the first-order Markov assumption behind equation (7), ξt\xi_tξt​ has mean zero conditional on that information, and ηt\eta_tηt​ is independent of all decisions. By the law of iterated expectations,

E[ktηt∗]=E[kt E[ξt+ηt∣information at t−1]]=0E[k_t\eta_t^*]=E\left[k_t\,E[\xi_t+\eta_t\mid\text{information at }t-1]\right]=0E[kt​ηt∗​]=E[kt​E[ξt​+ηt​∣information at t−1]]=0

Next the lagged intermediate input. By equation (10), ιt−1\iota_{t-1}ιt−1​ is a function of (ωt−1,kt−1)(\omega_{t-1},k_{t-1})(ωt−1​,kt−1​), which is also information dated t−1t-1t−1. The same argument gives

E[ιt−1ηt∗]=E[ιt−1 E[ξt+ηt∣information at t−1]]=0E[\iota_{t-1}\eta_t^*]=E\left[\iota_{t-1}\,E[\xi_t+\eta_t\mid\text{information at }t-1]\right]=0E[ιt−1​ηt∗​]=E[ιt−1​E[ξt​+ηt​∣information at t−1]]=0

The current intermediate input does not satisfy such a condition: ιt=ιt(ωt,kt)\iota_t=\iota_t(\omega_t,k_t)ιt​=ιt​(ωt​,kt​) with ωt=E[ωt∣ωt−1]+ξt\omega_t=E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]+\xi_tωt​=E[ωt​∣ωt−1​]+ξt​, so E[ιtξt]>0E[\iota_t\xi_t]>0E[ιt​ξt​]>0 under monotonicity.

Validity is not enough; the instrument must also be relevant. Conditional on ktk_tkt​ and on the control for E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​], the lagged input ιt−1\iota_{t-1}ιt−1​ must still predict ιt\iota_tιt​. The paper appeals to persistence in firm size and in ωt\omega_tωt​. With two parameters (βk,βι)(\beta_k,\beta_\iota)(βk​,βι​) in equation (12) and two moment conditions, the model is exactly identified; equation (26) adds over-identifying moments.

The firm's problem within a period is static. Capital KKK is fixed and productivity ω\omegaω is observed before the variable inputs are chosen. The firm is a price taker, with output price normalized to one and input prices pLp_LpL​ and pιp_\iotapι​. In this section LLL and ι\iotaι are levels, not logs. Profit is

π(L,ι)=f(K,L,ι,ω)−pLL−pιι\pi(L,\iota)=f(K,L,\iota,\omega)-p_L L-p_\iota\iotaπ(L,ι)=f(K,L,ι,ω)−pL​L−pι​ι

The firm chooses LLL and ι\iotaι to maximize π\piπ. At an interior optimum both partial derivatives vanish:

∂π∂L=fL(K,L,ι,ω)−pL=0,∂π∂ι=fι(K,L,ι,ω)−pι=0\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial L}=f_L(K,L,\iota,\omega)-p_L=0,\qquad \frac{\partial\pi}{\partial\iota}=f_\iota(K,L,\iota,\omega)-p_\iota=0∂L∂π​=fL​(K,L,ι,ω)−pL​=0,∂ι∂π​=fι​(K,L,ι,ω)−pι​=0

Rearranging gives the target: each variable input is used until its marginal product equals its real price. The second-order condition for a maximum is that the Hessian of π\piπ in (L,ι)(L,\iota)(L,ι), which equals the Hessian of fff in these two inputs, is negative definite:

fLL<0,fιι<0,fLLfιι−fιL2>0f_{LL}<0,\qquad f_{\iota\iota}<0,\qquad f_{LL}f_{\iota\iota}-f_{\iota L}^2>0fLL​<0,fιι​<0,fLL​fιι​−fιL2​>0

The two first-order conditions are two equations in the two unknowns (L,ι)(L,\iota)(L,ι). Their solution defines the input demand functions L(ω;pL,pι,K)L(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)L(ω;pL​,pι​,K) and ι(ω;pL,pι,K)\iota(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)ι(ω;pL​,pι​,K). The paper does not write the first-order conditions; it states only the sign result of equation (17) and refers to Varian (1992). They are the natural starting point for that result and are used in equation (15).

Start from the first-order conditions in equation (14), evaluated at the optimal choices, which are functions of ω\omegaω for given (pL,pι,K)(p_L,p_\iota,K)(pL​,pι​,K):

fL(K,L(ω),ι(ω),ω)=pL,fι(K,L(ω),ι(ω),ω)=pιf_L\left(K,L(\omega),\iota(\omega),\omega\right)=p_L,\qquad f_\iota\left(K,L(\omega),\iota(\omega),\omega\right)=p_\iotafL​(K,L(ω),ι(ω),ω)=pL​,fι​(K,L(ω),ι(ω),ω)=pι​

These hold as identities in ω\omegaω, so they can be differentiated with respect to ω\omegaω with KKK, pLp_LpL​ and pιp_\iotapι​ held fixed. The right-hand sides are constants, so their derivatives are zero. On the left, ω\omegaω acts through three channels: through L(ω)L(\omega)L(ω), through ι(ω)\iota(\omega)ι(ω) and directly. By the chain rule the first condition gives

fLL∂L∂ω+fLι∂ι∂ω+fLω=0f_{LL}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\omega}+f_{L\iota}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}+f_{L\omega}=0fLL​∂ω∂L​+fLι​∂ω∂ι​+fLω​=0

and the second gives

fιL∂L∂ω+fιι∂ι∂ω+fιω=0f_{\iota L}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\omega}+f_{\iota\iota}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}+f_{\iota\omega}=0fιL​∂ω∂L​+fιι​∂ω∂ι​+fιω​=0

Start from the closed form in equation (16). The sign of a ratio is the sign of the numerator times the sign of the denominator, so the denominator has to be signed. It is the determinant of the Hessian of the profit function in (L,ι)(L,\iota)(L,ι). At a strict interior maximum this Hessian is negative definite, which for a two-by-two matrix means a negative first diagonal element and a positive determinant:

fLL<0,fLLfιι−fιL2>0f_{LL}<0,\qquad f_{LL}f_{\iota\iota}-f_{\iota L}^2>0fLL​<0,fLL​fιι​−fιL2​>0

With a positive denominator,

sign(∂ι∂ω)=sign(fιLfLω−fLLfιωfLLfιι−fιL2)=sign(fιLfLω−fLLfιω)\text{sign}\left(\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}\right)=\text{sign}\left(\frac{f_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}}{f_{LL}f_{\iota\iota}-f_{\iota L}^2}\right)=\text{sign}\left(f_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}\right)sign(∂ω∂ι​)=sign(fLL​fιι​−fιL2​fιL​fLω​−fLL​fιω​​)=sign(fιL​fLω​−fLL​fιω​)

This is the only part of the argument that the paper prints (its equation (9) and the proof in its Appendix A, with a reference to Varian, 1992); equations (14) to (16) of the note reconstruct the steps behind it and agree with the paper's sign condition.

One point is left implicit in both the paper and the note. The necessary second-order condition only gives a negative semi-definite Hessian, so a determinant that is weakly positive. The strict inequality is an additional regularity assumption; it holds, for example, when fff is strictly concave in (L,ι)(L,\iota)(L,ι), which is decreasing returns to the variable inputs for fixed capital.

Reading the condition: −fLLfιω-f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}−fLL​fιω​ is the direct effect (productivity raises the marginal product of the intermediate input, scaled by how fast the marginal product of labour declines), and fιLfLωf_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}fιL​fLω​ is the indirect effect through labour (productivity raises labour, which raises or lowers the marginal product of the intermediate input depending on the sign of fιLf_{\iota L}fιL​). For Cobb-Douglas the numerator computed under equation (16) is βlβιf2/(L2ι)>0\beta_l\beta_\iota f^2/(L^2\iota)>0βl​βι​f2/(L2ι)>0, so the condition holds.

Fix prices and capital and regard the demand for the intermediate input as a function of ω\omegaω alone. By the implicit function theorem applied to equation (14) it is continuously differentiable, with derivative given by equation (16). The fundamental theorem of calculus then expresses the difference between demand at two productivity levels as the integral of the derivative:

ι(ω2;pL,pι,K)−ι(ω1;pL,pι,K)=∫ω1ω2∂ι∂ω(ω;pL,pι,K) dω\iota(\omega_2;p_L,p_\iota,K)-\iota(\omega_1;p_L,p_\iota,K)=\int_{\omega_1}^{\omega_2}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)\,d\omegaι(ω2​;pL​,pι​,K)−ι(ω1​;pL​,pι​,K)=∫ω1​ω2​​∂ω∂ι​(ω;pL​,pι​,K)dω

By hypothesis fιLfLω>fLLfιωf_{\iota L}f_{L\omega}>f_{LL}f_{\iota\omega}fιL​fLω​>fLL​fιω​ everywhere. By equation (17) this means that the integrand is strictly positive at every ω\omegaω in the interval. The integral of a strictly positive continuous function over an interval of positive length ω2−ω1>0\omega_2-\omega_1>0ω2​−ω1​>0 is strictly positive:

∫ω1ω2∂ι∂ω(ω;pL,pι,K) dω>∫ω1ω20 dω=0\int_{\omega_1}^{\omega_2}\frac{\partial\iota}{\partial\omega}(\omega;p_L,p_\iota,K)\,d\omega>\int_{\omega_1}^{\omega_2}0\,d\omega=0∫ω1​ω2​​∂ω∂ι​(ω;pL​,pι​,K)dω>∫ω1​ω2​​0dω=0

Therefore ι(ω2;pL,pι,K)>ι(ω1;pL,pι,K)\iota(\omega_2;p_L,p_\iota,K)>\iota(\omega_1;p_L,p_\iota,K)ι(ω2​;pL​,pι​,K)>ι(ω1​;pL​,pι​,K) whenever ω2>ω1\omega_2>\omega_1ω2​>ω1​: demand is strictly increasing in productivity, so for given KKK and prices each level of the input corresponds to exactly one ω\omegaω and the inversion used in equation (11) is legitimate.

The paper's Appendix A writes the integral with respect to the conditional distribution of productivity, P(dω∣K)P(d\omega\mid K)P(dω∣K), in place of dωd\omegadω. The note's version with ordinary integration is the correct statement of the fundamental theorem of calculus and does not need the distribution to put positive mass on the interval. The word "everywhere" matters: the condition has to hold along the whole path of optimal bundles between ω1\omega_1ω1​ and ω2\omega_2ω2​, not only at one point, and the strict second-order condition is needed along that path as well.

This is the perpetual inventory rule used to build the capital variable. The index jjj runs over three types of capital: buildings, machinery and vehicles. KjtK_{jt}Kjt​ is the real stock of type jjj at time ttt in 1980 pesos, δj\delta_jδj​ is its annual depreciation rate (0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 respectively) and ijti_{jt}ijt​ is real investment in that type during year ttt. A fraction 1−δj1-\delta_j1−δj​ of last year's stock survives, and this year's investment is added. The total KtK_tKt​ is the sum over types, and its log is the regressor ktk_tkt​ in equation (20).

Iterating the rule backwards shows that the stock is a depreciation-weighted sum of past investment:

Kjt=(1−δj)tKj0+∑s=0t−1(1−δj)sij,t−sK_{jt}=(1-\delta_j)^{t}K_{j0}+\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(1-\delta_j)^{s}i_{j,t-s}Kjt​=(1−δj​)tKj0​+s=0∑t−1​(1−δj​)sij,t−s​

For example, 100 of machinery with δj=0.10\delta_j=0.10δj​=0.10 and investment of 15 gives 0.9×100+15=1050.9\times 100+15=1050.9×100+15=105.

The important detail is timing. Here ijti_{jt}ijt​ enters KjtK_{jt}Kjt​ in the same period, whereas Olley and Pakes use Kt=(1−δ)Kt−1+it−1K_{t}=(1-\delta)K_{t-1}+i_{t-1}Kt​=(1−δ)Kt−1​+it−1​. The second stage needs capital to be uncorrelated with the innovation ξt\xi_tξt​ of equation (7); see equations (13) and (23). With contemporaneous investment in the stock, this requires that ijti_{jt}ijt​ be decided knowing only ωt−1\omega_{t-1}ωt−1​. If investment in year ttt responded to ξt\xi_tξt​, then ktk_tkt​ would be correlated with the second-stage error and βk\beta_kβk​ would be biased upwards. The paper acknowledges that the choice between the two timing conventions is somewhat arbitrary given what is known about the data.

This is the estimating version of equation (9): a Cobb-Douglas gross-output production function in logs with six inputs. yty_tyt​ is log real gross revenue, ktk_tkt​ log capital, ltsl_t^slts​ and ltul_t^ultu​ log skilled (white-collar) and unskilled (blue-collar) labour in man-years, and ete_tet​, ftf_tft​ and mtm_tmt​ log electricity, fuels and materials. Note that ftf_tft​ here is fuels and has nothing to do with the technology fff of equation (14). Each β\betaβ is an output elasticity, and their sum

βk+βs+βu+βe+βf+βm\beta_k+\beta_s+\beta_u+\beta_e+\beta_f+\beta_mβk​+βs​+βu​+βe​+βf​+βm​

measures returns to scale; a value of one is constant returns.

The inputs fall into three groups with different treatment. Capital is the state variable. Skilled and unskilled labour, electricity and fuels are freely variable inputs that are not the proxy; their coefficients are estimated in the first stage, equation (22). Materials is the freely variable input used as the proxy, so βm\beta_mβm​ is estimated in the second stage together with βk\beta_kβk​, equations (23) to (27). When electricity is the proxy, ete_tet​ and mtm_tmt​ exchange roles.

The Cobb-Douglas form is a first-order approximation, chosen to keep the exposition simple. It imposes unit elasticities of substitution and constant output elasticities across plants within an industry, which is why the model is estimated separately for each industry. The error terms are as in equation (3). Treating labour as freely variable rules out hiring and firing costs, which would make labour a state variable.

Start from equation (20). Materials demand is a function of the two state variables, as in equation (10) with mtm_tmt​ in the role of the intermediate input, mt=mt(ωt,kt)m_t=m_t(\omega_t,k_t)mt​=mt​(ωt​,kt​). Under the monotonicity condition of equation (17) it can be inverted to ωt=ωt(mt,kt)\omega_t=\omega_t(m_t,k_t)ωt​=ωt​(mt​,kt​). Substitute into equation (20):

yt=β0+βkkt+βslts+βultu+βeet+βfft+βmmt+ωt(mt,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_0+\beta_k k_t+\beta_s l_t^s+\beta_u l_t^u+\beta_e e_t+\beta_f f_t+\beta_m m_t+\omega_t(m_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=β0​+βk​kt​+βs​lts​+βu​ltu​+βe​et​+βf​ft​+βm​mt​+ωt​(mt​,kt​)+ηt​

ϕt(mt,kt)=β0+βmmt+βkkt+ωt(mt,kt)\phi_t(m_t,k_t)=\beta_0+\beta_m m_t+\beta_k k_t+\omega_t(m_t,k_t)ϕt​(mt​,kt​)=β0​+βm​mt​+βk​kt​+ωt​(mt​,kt​)

yt=βslts+βultu+βeet+βfft+ϕt(mt,kt)+ηty_t=\beta_s l_t^s+\beta_u l_t^u+\beta_e e_t+\beta_f f_t+\phi_t(m_t,k_t)+\eta_tyt​=βs​lts​+βu​ltu​+βe​et​+βf​ft​+ϕt​(mt​,kt​)+ηt​

This is a partially linear model with four linear regressors and an unknown function of two variables. The subscript on ϕt\phi_tϕt​ indicates that the function may shift over time; in the application a separate function is used for each of the periods 1979 to 1981, 1982 to 1983 and 1984 to 1986, because the inverse demand depends on prices and macroeconomic conditions that changed sharply over the cycle. The function ϕt(mt,kt)\phi_t(m_t,k_t)ϕt​(mt​,kt​) is known given the conditioning variables, and ηt\eta_tηt​ is mean independent of them, E(ηt∣kt,mt)=0E(\eta_t\mid k_t,m_t)=0E(ηt​∣kt​,mt​)=0, because it affects no decision. Therefore

yt−E(yt∣kt,mt)=βs(lts−E(lts∣kt,mt))+βu(ltu−E(ltu∣kt,mt))+βe(et−E(et∣kt,mt))+βf(ft−E(ft∣kt,mt))+ηt\begin{aligned} y_t-E(y_t\mid k_t,m_t)={}&\beta_s\left(l_t^s-E(l_t^s\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\beta_u\left(l_t^u-E(l_t^u\mid k_t,m_t)\right) \\ &+\beta_e\left(e_t-E(e_t\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\beta_f\left(f_t-E(f_t\mid k_t,m_t)\right)+\eta_t \end{aligned}yt​−E(yt​∣kt​,mt​)=​βs​(lts​−E(lts​∣kt​,mt​))+βu​(ltu​−E(ltu​∣kt​,mt​))+βe​(et​−E(et​∣kt​,mt​))+βf​(ft​−E(ft​∣kt​,mt​))+ηt​​

This is the target, the four-regressor version of equation (6). The five conditional means are estimated by locally weighted quadratic regressions on (kt,mt)(k_t,m_t)(kt​,mt​), and no-intercept OLS of the output residual on the four input residuals estimates the four coefficients consistently, since ηt\eta_tηt​ is uncorrelated with the inputs and with any function of (kt,mt)(k_t,m_t)(kt​,mt​).

As in equation (6), an unstated requirement is that the four residualized inputs have variation that is not explained by (kt,mt)(k_t,m_t)(kt​,mt​). If labour, electricity and fuels were all exact functions of (ωt,kt)(\omega_t,k_t)(ωt​,kt​) like materials, each would be an exact function of (mt,kt)(m_t,k_t)(mt​,kt​), the regressors would be identically zero and the first stage would identify nothing. Identification comes from whatever moves these inputs apart from materials for given capital.

This is the objective function of the second stage. For each instrument h=1,…,8h=1,\ldots,8h=1,…,8 define the sample moment

The paper prints the left-hand side as Q(β∗)Q(\beta^*)Q(β∗) and the right-hand side with min⁡β∗\min_{\beta^*}minβ∗​ in front of the sum, which mixes up the function and its minimized value; the note's form, a function of the candidate β∗\beta^*β∗ that is then minimized, is the correct reading.

Several features are worth noting. The eight moments get equal weights (an identity weighting matrix), so the estimator is consistent but not efficient, and the relative scale of the instruments affects how much each moment counts. The sums are not divided by the number of observations, which does not change the minimizer. With eight moments and two parameters, QQQ is generally positive at the minimum, and its minimized value is the basis of the over-identification test, with a bootstrap distribution. The sum over ttt starts at Ti0T_{i0}Ti0​, the second year a firm is observed, because the residual needs ω^t−1\hat{\omega}_{t-1}ω^t−1​ from equation (25). The criterion is not quadratic in β∗\beta^*β∗, since β∗\beta^*β∗ also enters the non-parametric estimate of E[ωt∣ωt−1]E[\omega_t\mid\omega_{t-1}]E[ωt​∣ωt−1​], and it can have several local minima; this is why a grid search is used.

The short-cut replaces the estimation of the proxy's coefficient by an observed revenue share. Let PPP be the output price and write the levels of output and of the intermediate input as eyte^{y_t}eyt​ and eιte^{\iota_t}eιt​. A cost-minimizing price taker uses the intermediate input until the value of its marginal product equals its price:

P ∂eyt∂eιt=pιP\,\frac{\partial e^{y_t}}{\partial e^{\iota_t}}=p_\iotaP∂eιt​∂eyt​​=pι​

Multiply both sides by eιt/(Peyt)e^{\iota_t}/(Pe^{y_t})eιt​/(Peyt​). The left-hand side becomes the output elasticity of the input and the right-hand side its share in revenue:

∂yt∂ιt=pιeιtPeyt=sι\frac{\partial y_t}{\partial\iota_t}=\frac{p_\iota e^{\iota_t}}{Pe^{y_t}}=s_\iota∂ιt​∂yt​​=Peyt​pι​eιt​​=sι​

In the log-linear production function of equation (9) the elasticity is the constant βι\beta_\iotaβι​, so

Suppressing the intercept, which is absorbed by the unrestricted conditional expectation, gives the target. Only βk\beta_kβk​ is left, and the single moment E[ktηt∗]=0E[k_t\eta_t^*]=0E[kt​ηt∗​]=0 from equation (13) identifies it; no instrument for ιt\iota_tιt​ is needed.

Two unstated qualifications. First, the input is chosen before ηt\eta_tηt​ is realized, so the first-order condition holds for expected output; the observed share of an individual plant equals βι\beta_\iotaβι​ times a factor E[eηt]/eηtE[e^{\eta_t}]/e^{\eta_t}E[eηt​]/eηt​, and sιs_\iotasι​ should be read as an average share across plants, not a plant-specific one. Second, the equality of the elasticity and the share uses price-taking in the output market and no adjustment frictions for the input; with a markup the share understates the elasticity. Separability in the proxy input is what allows its contribution to be subtracted from output without affecting the form of the rest of the production function.

This is the starting model of the Blundell and Bond (2000) estimator, one of the alternatives against which the intermediate input estimator is compared. It is written in their notation, which clashes with the rest of the note: here ηi\eta_iηi​ is a time-invariant firm effect, not the i.i.d. shock ηt\eta_tηt​, and mitm_{it}mit​ is measurement error, not materials.

The terms are: yity_{it}yit​ log output, xitx_{it}xit​ the vector of log inputs with coefficient vector β\betaβ, γt\gamma_tγt​ a year effect common to all firms, ηi\eta_iηi​ a firm fixed effect, vitv_{it}vit​ a persistent productivity shock that follows an AR(1) process vit=ρvi,t−1+eitv_{it}=\rho v_{i,t-1}+e_{it}vit​=ρvi,t−1​+eit​, and mitm_{it}mit​ a serially uncorrelated (MA(0)) measurement error. The productivity term that inputs respond to is ηi+vit\eta_i+v_{it}ηi​+vit​, the counterpart of ωt\omega_tωt​ in equation (3), restricted to a fixed effect plus a linear AR(1) process, whereas equation (7) allows any first-order Markov process.

The AR(1) structure permits quasi-differencing: subtracting ρ\rhoρ times the lagged equation removes vitv_{it}vit​ and gives a dynamic model with a restricted set of coefficients,

yit=ρyi,t−1+β′xit−ρβ′xi,t−1+(γt−ργt−1)+(1−ρ)ηi+eit+mit−ρmi,t−1y_{it}=\rho y_{i,t-1}+\beta' x_{it}-\rho\beta' x_{i,t-1}+(\gamma_t-\rho\gamma_{t-1})+(1-\rho)\eta_i+e_{it}+m_{it}-\rho m_{i,t-1}yit​=ρyi,t−1​+β′xit​−ρβ′xi,t−1​+(γt​−ργt−1​)+(1−ρ)ηi​+eit​+mit​−ρmi,t−1​

First-differencing removes (1−ρ)ηi(1-\rho)\eta_i(1−ρ)ηi​, and sufficiently lagged levels of inputs and output serve as instruments for the differenced equation, while lagged first differences serve as instruments for the equation in levels (system GMM). Identification comes from the assumption that the innovation eite_{it}eit​ is unpredictable from lagged choices, similar in spirit to equation (26), but no proxy is used and no monotonicity is needed. In the Chilean data the estimates were unstable across bootstrap samples and often at the boundary of the parameter space, so they are not reported.
